# Part C: Resampling structured data

Part A treated the 731 days as independent. C.1 asks whether 2012 was warmer
than 2011, using the block bootstrap to keep nearby days together. C.2
compares three ways to bootstrap a regression slope when the error variance
changes with $x$, then resamples within each year to compare the two years.

## C.1(a): A seasonal cycle and its residuals

Temperature is not stationary: it follows a yearly cycle. Model it as a cycle
plus a 2012 effect plus stationary noise $Z_t$,
$$\text{temp}_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \, \text{y2012}_t + \text{cycle}(d_t) + Z_t,$$
where $d_t$ is the day of the year and y2012 is 1 for days in 2012. The code
below fits the model. The sines and cosines fit a smooth yearly cycle.

```{r cycle}
bikes$y2012 <- as.numeric(bikes$year == 2012)
bikes$d <- as.numeric(format(as.Date(bikes$date), "%j"))   # day of the year
fit_temp <- lm(temp ~ y2012 + sin(2 * pi * d / 365) + cos(2 * pi * d / 365) +
                 sin(4 * pi * d / 365) + cos(4 * pi * d / 365), data = bikes)
z <- resid(fit_temp)
ggplot(data.frame(date = as.Date(bikes$date), temp = bikes$temp,
                  fitted = fitted(fit_temp)), aes(date, temp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) + geom_line(aes(y = fitted))
```

1. Report the coefficient of `y2012` and its SE from `summary(fit_temp)`.
2. Compute the lag-1 autocorrelation of the residuals `z`, and the
   autocorrelations to lag 14. By about which lag are they near 0?

## C.1(b): The block bootstrap

`block_boot` is the moving block bootstrap from the deck. `effect(zs)` adds a
resampled residual series `zs` to the fitted values and returns the refitted
`y2012` coefficient. `lm.fit` refits with the same columns much faster than
`lm`.

```{r block-fns}
block_boot <- function(x, stat, B, l) {
  n <- length(x)
  replicate(B, {
    xs <- c()
    while (length(xs) < n) {
      i <- sample(n - l + 1, 1)
      xs <- c(xs, x[i:(i + l - 1)])
    }
    stat(xs[1:n])
  })
}
X <- model.matrix(fit_temp)
effect <- function(zs) coef(lm.fit(X, fitted(fit_temp) + zs))[["y2012"]]
```

1. Compute the block bootstrap SE of the 2012 effect for
   `ls <- c(1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 14, 21, 30, 45)` with $B = 2000$, and plot it
   against $\ell$.
2. Which $\ell$ gives about the SE from `summary`, and why? Choose an $\ell$
   where the SE has leveled off.
3. Report the 95% normal interval for the 2012 effect with your $\ell$, and
   with the SE from `summary`. Was 2012 warmer than 2011?

## C.2(a): Three bootstraps for a slope

Now fit `casual ~ temp` to all days. As in Part A, treat the days as
independent.

```{r casual}
fit_casual <- lm(casual ~ temp, data = bikes)
x <- bikes$temp
y <- bikes$casual
y_hat <- fitted(fit_casual)
e <- resid(fit_casual)
ggplot(data.frame(temp = x, e), aes(temp, e)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2)
far <- order(-abs(x - mean(x)))[1:10]   # the 10 days farthest from the mean temp
```

The spread of the residuals grows with temperature.

1. Bootstrap the slope `cov(x, y) / var(x)` with $B = 2000$ by resampling
   cases, resampling errors, and the wild bootstrap. Report the three SEs
   and the SE from `summary(fit_casual)`.
2. The days farthest from the mean temperature have the most influence on
   the slope. Compare the mean $|e_i|$ for the 10 days in `far` with the mean
   $|e_i|$ for all days.
3. Use (2) to explain why resampling errors disagrees with the wild
   bootstrap here.

## C.2(b): Comparing the two years

Did ridership grow from 2011 to 2012? Treat the two years as strata.
`bikes |> group_by(year) |> slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE)` draws one
bootstrap sample that resamples days within each year.

1. Compute the median of `total` in each year, and the difference, 2012
   minus 2011.
2. Bootstrap the difference with $B = 2000$, resampling days within each
   year.
3. Report the bootstrap SE and the 95% percentile interval. Why resample
   within each year rather than all 731 days?
